title: Jensen Huang Returns as Washington Tightens Its Grip on AI
summary: Huang's return preserves an influential advocate for open models, but Washington's efforts to secure American AI leadership could ultimately leave its future concentrated among fewer companies.
body_markdown:
This article originally appeared in Galaxy Research's weekly newsletter.[Subscribe](https://www.galaxy.com/subscribe-to-research?utm_campaign=Weekly%20Research%20Brief%20-%20Email&utm_medium=email&utm_source=hs_email&_hsenc=p2ANqtz--YWOkviRZJsa_uYNPjl2N4ahqTpHeV86Rs9VQQeL9MWn1U09L_xNxjRhoRyGaaBrCPLXuX) to get timely insights delivered to your inbox every Friday morning.


#### WHAT HAPPENED


[Nvidia announced](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000104581026000090/nov23pressrelease.htm) **Monday that its board had unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and director, less than two weeks after his resignation amid reports that he may have been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.** Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who had served as interim CEO, returned to her previous role. Harvey Jones remained board chair.


Nvidia said the board received input from senior U.S. government officials and concluded that Huang's return posed no national security risk.[President Donald Trump](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/nvidia-jensen-huang-trump-comment-national-security-risk/) said he had personally pushed for the decision. An independent board investigation remains ongoing. Nvidia also established a national security and export-control committee and said it would hire a chief compliance officer.


[Nvidia shares jumped 31.5%](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/wall-street-futures-rebound-after-rough-week-for-ailinked-shares-5044594) on the news of Huang’s reinstatement, adding roughly $950 billion in market value, while the Nasdaq rose 6.5%. The same day, the Commerce Department[blacklisted Singapore-based Megaspeed](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/us-to-blacklist-megaspeed-chip-firm-linked-to-nvidia-scandal-source-says-5046337) , a cloud provider under investigation over alleged diversion of U.S. chips to China. Huang is[scheduled to testify](https://www.banking.senate.gov/hearings/protecting-americas-ai-advantage-oversight-of-us-export-controls) about U.S. chip export controls before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.


#### OUR TAKE


In his 2024 essay[Situational Awareness](https://situational-awareness.ai/the-project/) , Leopold Aschenbrenner predicted that the discovery of Chinese infiltration at a leading U.S. AI lab could help trigger a government-directed AI project by 2027 or 2028. This month, the head of the company supplying much of the hardware for that race resigned amid reports of a possible foreign intelligence effort. Washington stepped in, and he got his job back.


Nvidia isn't a frontier model lab, and the allegations surrounding Huang remain under investigation. Still, the episode supports Aschenbrenner's broader prediction that AI's strategic importance would draw the national security state more deeply into its development. In Nvidia's case, the administration intervened to preserve continuity at the private company powering much of the AI buildout. A corporate leadership decision became a matter of national economic importance, reinforcing just how dependent the broader AI ecosystem has become on Nvidia.


Priorities within Washington aren't entirely aligned, however. The administration supported Huang's reinstatement even as the Commerce Department tightened restrictions on access to Nvidia's chips. A[new rule](https://www.bis.gov/press-release/bis-issues-rule-addressing-remote-access-american-super-intelligence-technology) targets remote access to advanced U.S. computing capacity through overseas data centers, while the Megaspeed blacklist addresses an alleged route for diverting chips to China. Meanwhile, lawmakers from both parties are demanding answers about export compliance and the administration's role in the board's reversal. Huang is back in charge, but Nvidia's ability to serve Chinese demand through foreign intermediaries is narrowing.


These restrictions have implications for open-weight AI, an area Huang has[championed](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/jensen-huang-nvidia-resignation-open-weight-ai-hugging-face-china-spy-megaspeed) . Nvidia has a clear commercial incentive to support models that developers can download and modify. Making advanced models more accessible expands the number of companies building AI applications, creating a broader market for its hardware and software. That strategy includes its[pending $12.93 billion acquisition of Hugging Face](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-to-acquire-hugging-face/) , a leading platform for distributing open models. Huang's return keeps one of the industry's most vocal open-weight advocates in charge, although[Nvidia reaffirmed its commitment](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/17/nvidia-says-its-open-source-ai-strategy-remains-intact-after-jensen-huangs-exit/) to the strategy during his absence.


The complication is that some of the most competitive open-weight models come from China, and their contributions extend beyond Chinese developers. Chinese labs have released open-source software such as DeepSeek's DeepGEMM and DeepEP, which have been incorporated into Western AI infrastructure, including frameworks such as[vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/utils/import_utils.py) . Restricting access to U.S. computing capacity could slow future Chinese model development, but also reduce contributions to the broader open-source ecosystem. Tighter controls may also accelerate China's shift toward domestic chips, weakening Nvidia's longer-term influence over Chinese AI development.


A[new House committee report](https://homeland.house.gov/2026/11/20/chairmen-garbarino-moolenaar-release-joint-investigative-report-urging-removal-of-prc-open-weight-models-from-federal-systems-high-risk-critical-infrastructure/) calls for removing Chinese models from federal systems while encouraging competitive American alternatives. The report also acknowledges that the U.S. lacks open-weight alternatives matching Chinese offerings on price and performance. This creates a potential unintended consequence. If restrictions slow Chinese open-weight development before American alternatives can close the gap, developers could become more dependent on proprietary models from the frontier labs, OpenAI and Anthropic. Rather than broadening access to advanced AI, the restrictions could further concentrate influence over its development among a handful of companies.


Beyond open models, Huang's return leaves other fundamental questions unanswered. The industry continues to commit enormous sums to data center infrastructure on future demand that is modeled but not entirely confirmed. Meanwhile, increasingly capable models raise concerns about cybersecurity and potentially catastrophic outcomes, risks highlighted in[Anthropic's IPO filing](https://www.galaxy.com/insights/research/anthropic-record-ipo-ant-hyperliquid) last week. Restoring Huang provides continuity for Nvidia, but does little to resolve these uncertainties.


Aschenbrenner envisioned foreign infiltration pushing Washington toward a government-directed AI project. We're not there, but government involvement in AI is taking several forms. Last year, Washington[acquired a 9.9% stake in Intel](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/newsroom/news/corporate/intel-and-trump-administration-reach-historic-agreement.html) , while OpenAI has reportedly[discussed giving the government a 5% stake](https://www.ft.com/content/0a718201-cee1-4447-8fb5-6835f1441a96) . This week, Trump[floated the possibility](https://nypost.com/2026/11/24/us-news/trump-leaves-door-open-to-jensen-huang-pardon-and-urges-him-not-to-plead-5th-to-congress-next-week/) of Uncle Sam taking a stake in Nvidia. Together with the administration's involvement in Huang's reinstatement and its tightening export restrictions, these developments suggest Washington is becoming more willing to shape AI development through direct engagement with private companies.


That raises a further question for open models. If restrictions weaken Chinese competitors before American alternatives can close the gap, OpenAI and Anthropic could gain even greater influence over AI's direction.


Huang's return preserves an influential advocate for open models, but Washington's efforts to secure American AI leadership could ultimately leave its future concentrated among fewer companies.
